units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Comparing and adding fractions
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Mathematics: Common fractions (compare and order to twelfths, add and subtract with the same denominator, mixed numbers, fractions of whole numbers)
units.intention: Today I am practising comparing and adding fractions.
units.prompt: How did you decide which is bigger?

lesson.say: In three eighths, the bottom number says the whole is cut into 8 equal parts. The top number says we have 3 of them.
lesson.html: In the fraction 3/8, the denominator (8) says the whole is cut into 8 equal parts. The numerator (3) says how many parts we have.

lesson.say: With the same denominator, compare the numerators. With the same numerator, the smaller denominator gives bigger parts.
lesson.html:
Same denominator: compare the numerators. 5/8 is more than 3/8.

Same numerator: the smaller denominator gives bigger parts. 1/3 is more than 1/6.

lesson.h: Adding and finding a fraction of a number
lesson.say: To add fractions with the same denominator, add the numerators. To find three quarters of 20, divide by 4 then multiply by 3.
lesson.html:
Adding: when the denominators are the same, add the numerators and keep the denominator: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.

Fraction of a number: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 3/4 of 20 = (20 ÷ 4) × 3 = 15.

Mixed numbers: 7/4 is one whole (4/4) and 3/4 more, so 7/4 = 1¾.

steps: Divide by the denominator: 30 ÷ 5 = 6. So 1/5 of 30 is 6.
Multiply by the numerator: 6 × 2 = 12.
So 2/5 of 30 is 12.

questions.q: Which fraction is bigger: 1/4 or 1/10?
hints: Both have 1 part. Which part is bigger?
Think of a pizza cut into 4 slices and one cut into 10 slices.
questions.explain: A quarter is bigger than a tenth, because the whole is cut into fewer parts.
3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8. We add the parts; their size does not change.

questions.q: Put these fractions in order from smallest to biggest.
hints: All of these have 1 as the numerator.
The bigger the denominator, the smaller each part.
Twelfths are the smallest parts and halves are the biggest.
questions.explain: 1/12 is smaller than 1/5, and 1/5 is smaller than 1/2.

questions.q: What is 3/4 of 24?
Sipho ate 2/6 of a pizza and Lerato ate 3/6. How much did they eat altogether?
hints: The pizza slices are the same size.
Add the numerators and keep the denominator.
questions.explain: 2/6 + 3/6 = 5/6. One slice is left.

questions.q: Which mixed number is the same as 7/4?
hints: How many quarters make one whole?
4 quarters make 1 whole. How many quarters are left over?
7 − 4 = 3, so it is 1 whole and 3 quarters.

units.parent: Your child compared, ordered and added fractions, and found fractions of whole numbers.
units.teacher: Shows whether the learner reasons about part size when comparing, adds like fractions correctly and uses the divide-then-multiply strategy.
units.done: Fractions help us share fairly, cook, measure and tell the time.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Information text: African penguins
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 English Home Language, Term 1: Information text with visuals (reading and viewing); language structures: verbs and tense
units.intention: Today I am practising finding information in a text and using verbs correctly.
units.prompt: Where in the text did you find that?
units.passage:
African Penguins

Where they live. African penguins live along the coasts of South Africa and Namibia. One of the best places to see them is Boulders Beach, near Simon's Town in the Western Cape.

What they look like. An African penguin is about 60 centimetres tall. It has a black back, a white front and a black stripe across its chest. Above each eye there is a patch of pink skin. The pink patches help the penguin to lose heat when it is hot.

What they eat. African penguins are strong, fast swimmers. They dive into the sea to catch small fish, such as sardines and anchovies.

A loud call. African penguins make a loud call that sounds like a donkey braying.

Why they need help. There are far fewer African penguins today than there were a hundred years ago. Many people are working to protect them and the fish they eat.

Fact box
Height: about 60 cm
Food: small fish
Home: the coasts of South Africa and Namibia

lesson.say: An information text gives facts about a topic. It uses headings so you can find information quickly, and it is usually written in the present tense.
lesson.html:
An information text gives facts about a topic. It often has:

  • headings that help you find information quickly
  • visuals or a fact box
  • verbs in the present tense: penguins live, they eat

lesson.say: Read the text about African penguins.
lesson.html:
African Penguins

Where they live. African penguins live along the coasts of South Africa and Namibia. One of the best places to see them is Boulders Beach, near Simon's Town in the Western Cape.

What they look like. An African penguin is about 60 centimetres tall. It has a black back, a white front and a black stripe across its chest. Above each eye there is a patch of pink skin. The pink patches help the penguin to lose heat when it is hot.

What they eat. African penguins are strong, fast swimmers. They dive into the sea to catch small fish, such as sardines and anchovies.

A loud call. African penguins make a loud call that sounds like a donkey braying.

Why they need help. There are far fewer African penguins today than there were a hundred years ago. Many people are working to protect them and the fish they eat.

Fact box
Height: about 60 cm
Food: small fish
Home: the coasts of South Africa and Namibia

lesson.say: A verb is a doing or being word. Present tense tells what happens now or usually. Past tense tells what already happened.
lesson.html:
A verb is a doing or being word: swim, eat, is.

Present tense tells what happens now or usually: Penguins swim fast.

Past tense tells what already happened: The penguin swam to the rocks. Many past tense verbs end in -ed (dived, called), but some change (swim → swam, eat → ate).

example.q: Change to the past tense: "The penguin catches a fish."
steps: Find the verb: "catches".
The past tense of "catch" is "caught". It does not end in -ed.
"The penguin caught a fish."

questions.q: Where do African penguins live?
options: On the coasts of South Africa and Namibia
hints: Look under the heading "Where they live".
Read the first sentence of that part.
questions.explain: They live along the coasts of South Africa and Namibia.

questions.q: Why do African penguins have pink patches above their eyes?
hints: Look under the heading "What they look like".
Read the sentence after the one about pink skin.
questions.explain: The pink patches help the penguin lose heat when it is hot.

questions.q: Which heading would help you find what penguins eat?
hints: Headings tell you what each part is about.
Look for the heading with "eat" in it.
questions.explain: The heading "What they eat" tells you that part is about food.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the whole text?
options: Facts about African penguins and why they need help
A story about a lost penguin
hints: The main idea is what the whole text is about, not one detail.
Look at the title and all the headings.
Every part is about the same animal.
questions.explain: The whole text gives facts about African penguins and explains why they need help.

questions.q: Sort the verbs into present tense and past tense.
hints: Past tense tells what already happened.
Many past tense verbs end in -ed.
questions.explain: swim, eat and live are present tense. dived, called and caught are past tense.

questions.q: Choose the correct past tense: "Yesterday the penguin ___ into the sea."
questions.explain: "Yesterday" means the past, so we use "dived".

units.parent: Your child read an information text about African penguins, found facts using headings, and practised verbs in the present and past tense.
units.teacher: Shows use of text features (headings, fact box) to locate information, identification of the main idea, and control of verb tense, including irregular verbs.
units.done: Information texts help us learn about the world and find facts quickly.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Food chains
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 1, Life and Living: Food chains (producers, consumers, herbivores, carnivores, omnivores)
units.intention: Today I am practising showing how energy moves through living things.
units.prompt: What would happen if one part was missing?

lesson.say: Plants are producers. They make their own food using energy from the sun. Animals are consumers. They get energy by eating plants or other animals.
lesson.html:
Producers make their own food. Green plants are producers: they use energy from the sun.

Consumers get energy by eating. Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat animals. Omnivores eat plants and animals.

lesson.say: A food chain shows who eats what. The arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it. It shows the direction energy moves.
lesson.html:
grass→grasshopper→lizard→hawk

The arrow means "is eaten by". It points the way energy moves. Every food chain starts with a producer.

lesson.say: If one living thing in a food chain disappears, the others are affected. Living things depend on each other.
lesson.html: Living things depend on each other. If grasshoppers disappeared, lizards would have less food, and hawks might have fewer lizards to eat. Grass might grow taller with nothing eating it.

example.q: Build a food chain from: lion, grass, zebra.
steps: Find the producer first: grass makes its own food.
Who eats grass? The zebra, a herbivore.
Who eats the zebra? The lion, a carnivore. So: grass → zebra → lion.

questions.q: Put this food chain in order, starting with the producer.
hints: Which one makes its own food?
questions.explain: grass → springbok → cheetah.

questions.q: In a food chain, what does the arrow mean?
hints: Does the grass eat the grasshopper, or the other way round?
The arrow points to the eater.
questions.explain: The arrow means "is eaten by" and shows the direction energy moves.

questions.q: Sort the animals: herbivore, carnivore or omnivore.
hints: Herbivores eat only plants. Carnivores eat only animals.
Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Baboons eat fruit, roots and insects. Humans eat plants and meat.
questions.explain: Cows and zebras are herbivores, lions and eagles are carnivores, baboons and humans are omnivores.

questions.q: Where does the energy in every food chain first come from?
hints: How do green plants make food?
questions.explain: Green plants use energy from the sun to make food. That energy passes along the chain.

questions.q: In grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, what might happen if all the grasshoppers died?
hints: What happens when an animal loses its food?
Then think one step further along the chain.
questions.explain: Lizards would lose their food. Fewer lizards could then mean less food for hawks too.

questions.q: Which living thing is a producer?
questions.explain: The aloe is a plant, so it makes its own food. It is a producer.

reflect.q: What helped you understand food chains?

units.parent: Your child built food chains, sorted animals by what they eat, and thought about what happens when one part of a chain is missing.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of producers and consumers, the direction of energy flow, classification by diet and early systems thinking (knock-on effects).
units.done: Every living thing is part of a bigger system.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: Coping with emotions
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: coping with emotions
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Coping with emotions (anger, disappointment, sadness; empathy and compassion)
units.intention: Today I am practising naming feelings and finding healthy ways to cope.
units.prompt: What could help in that moment?

lesson.say: Everyone feels angry, disappointed or sad sometimes. Feelings are normal. What matters is what we do with them.
lesson.html: Everyone feels angry, disappointed or sad sometimes. Feelings are normal and they pass. What matters is what we do with them.

lesson.say: Healthy ways to cope include breathing slowly, taking a break, moving your body, and talking to someone you trust.
lesson.html:
• Breathe in slowly, then out slowly
  • Take a short break somewhere calm
  • Move your body: walk, stretch, jump
  • Draw or write about it
  • Talk to someone you trust

If you ever feel unsafe, or a feeling is too big to manage, tell a grown-up you trust.

lesson.say: Empathy means trying to understand how someone else feels. Compassion means wanting to help.
lesson.html: Empathy means trying to understand how someone else feels. Compassion means wanting to help them feel better.

example.q: Lebo's drawing was torn by accident. She feels angry. What could she do?
steps: First, name the feeling: "I feel angry."
Then calm her body: breathe slowly or step away for a moment.
Then talk about it, or decide whether to fix or redo the drawing.

questions.q: Sam was not chosen for the team. How might he feel?
hints: He hoped for something that did not happen.
This feeling comes when hopes are not met.
questions.explain: Not being chosen when you hoped to be can make you feel disappointed.

questions.q: Sort these ways of coping with anger.
hints: Helpful ways keep you and others safe.
Would it hurt someone or something?
Calming down and talking are helpful.
questions.explain: Breathing, taking a break and talking are helpful. Hurting, breaking and insulting are not.

questions.q: Your friend's pet died and they are sad. What shows empathy?
options: "I'm sorry. That must be really hard."
questions.explain: Saying you are sorry and that it must be hard shows you understand how they feel.

questions.q: What is a good first step when you feel a big emotion?
hints: Knowing what you feel helps you choose what to do.
Putting a name to it is the first step.
questions.explain: Naming the feeling helps you understand it and choose a healthy way to cope.

questions.q: Which person is the BEST to talk to when a feeling is too big?
hints: You want someone safe who can help.
Think of a parent, teacher or carer.
questions.explain: A trusted grown-up can listen and help you stay safe.

reflect.q: Which way of coping would you try?

units.parent: Your child practised naming feelings, choosing healthy ways to cope, and showing empathy. Nothing personal about their own feelings was recorded.
units.teacher: Uses scenarios only. Shows recognition of emotions, sorting of coping strategies, and empathic responses. No personal disclosures are requested or recorded.
units.done: Every feeling is allowed. You get to choose what you do with it.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Big numbers and rounding
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Mathematics: Whole numbers (place value to 6 digits; ordering and comparing; rounding to the nearest 5, 10, 100 and 1 000)
units.intention: Today I am practising reading big numbers and rounding them.
units.prompt: Which place did you look at first?

lesson.say: In 482 615, the 4 is worth 400 thousand and the 8 is worth 80 thousand.
lesson.html:
HThTThThHTU
482615

482 615 = 400 000 + 80 000 + 2 000 + 600 + 10 + 5. We read it as "four hundred and eighty-two thousand, six hundred and fifteen".

lesson.say: Numbers rounded to the nearest 5 end in 0 or 5. 73 rounds to 75, and 71 rounds to 70.
lesson.html:
Rounded to the nearest 5, a number ends in 0 or 5. 73 is closer to 75 than to 70, so it rounds to 75. 71 rounds to 70.

For 10, 100 and 1 000, use the same rule as before: look at the digit to the right. 5 or more rounds up.

steps: The thousands digit is 8, so the answer is 248 000 or 249 000.
Look at the hundreds digit: it is 6.
6 is 5 or more, so round up: 249 000.

questions.q: What is the value of the 8 in 482 615?
hints: The 8 is the second digit from the left.
It is in the ten thousands place.
questions.explain: The 8 is in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 80 000.

questions.q: Which number is 300 000 + 40 000 + 500 + 7?
hints: Put each part in its place.
There are no thousands and no tens.
3 hundred thousands, 4 ten thousands, 0 thousands, 5 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 units.

questions.q: Round 73 to the nearest 5.
hints: The answer must end in 0 or 5.
73 is 2 away from 75 and 3 away from 70.
questions.explain: 73 is closer to 75 than to 70.

questions.q: Round 248 637 to the nearest 100.
hints: The tens digit is 3, which is less than 5.
questions.explain: The tens digit is 3, so round down to 248 600.

questions.q: Put these in order from smallest to biggest.
hints: First count the digits. Fewer digits means a smaller number.
Then compare 405 120 and 450 012 by the ten thousands digit.
questions.explain: 45 120 is smallest. Then 405 120, then 450 012.

questions.q: A stadium has 58 386 seats. To the nearest 1 000, about how many seats is that?
hints: It is 3, which is less than 5.
questions.explain: The hundreds digit is 3, so round down to 58 000.

reflect.q: What helped you with big numbers?

units.parent: Your child read and compared six-digit numbers and rounded them in different ways.
units.teacher: Shows place value to 6 digits, expanded notation, rounding to 5, 10, 100 and 1 000, and ordering by digit count and place.
units.done: Big numbers are used for populations, distances and money.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Multiples and factors
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Mathematics: Whole numbers, properties of numbers (multiples and factors of 2-digit numbers to at least 100)
units.intention: Today I am practising finding multiples and factors.

lesson.say: Multiples of 4 are the numbers in the 4 times table: 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on.
lesson.html:
The multiples of 4 are the answers in the 4 times table:

4→8→12→16→20→…

A common multiple is in both lists. 12 is a common multiple of 3 and 4.

lesson.say: Factors are numbers that divide exactly into a number. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
lesson.html:
Factors divide into a number exactly, with nothing left over. Find them in pairs:

12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4, so the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.

The highest common factor of two numbers is the biggest factor they share.

steps: Start with 1: 1 × 18.
Try 2: 2 × 9. Try 3: 3 × 6. 4 and 5 do not divide 18 exactly.
The next would be 6, which we already have. So the factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.

questions.q: Which number is a multiple of 6?
questions.explain: 6 × 7 = 42, so 42 is a multiple of 6.

questions.q: Sort these numbers: factors of 20, or not?
questions.explain: 4, 5 and 10 are factors of 20. 6, 8 and 3 are not.

questions.q: How many factors does 16 have?
questions.explain: 16 has 5 factors: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.

questions.q: What is the biggest number that is a factor of both 12 and 18?
hints: List the factors of 12 and of 18.
Which is the biggest one in both lists?
questions.explain: 6 is the highest common factor of 12 and 18.

questions.q: Chairs are put out in rows of 7. Which number of chairs makes full rows with none left over?
questions.explain: 63 = 7 × 9, so 63 chairs make 9 full rows.

questions.q: Which number is a common multiple of 3 and 4?
hints: It must be in the 3 times table and the 4 times table.
Which of these is also a multiple of 3?
questions.explain: 24 is 3 × 8 and 4 × 6, so it is a common multiple.

units.parent: Your child found multiples and factors, including ones that two numbers share.
units.teacher: Shows systematic search for factor pairs, recall of multiplication facts, and common multiples and factors.
units.done: Factors help with sharing, grouping and simplifying fractions.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Newspaper report: Beach clean-up
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 English Home Language, Term 1: Newspaper or magazine article (reading and viewing); direct speech
units.intention: Today I am practising finding the key facts in a news report.
units.prompt: Which W did you find first?
units.passage:
A made-up news report for this lesson

Learners collect 300 kg of litter from beach

By a Seaview Times reporter

Grade 5 learners from Seaview Primary School collected 300 kilograms of litter from the beach near their school last Saturday morning.

The 64 learners spent three hours picking up plastic bottles, bottle tops and fishing line. They wanted to protect the birds and fish that live along the coast.

"We found a seagull tangled in fishing line, and a lifeguard helped to free it," said learner Amahle Dube. "That is when we knew our work really mattered."

The school plans to clean the beach again next term.

lesson.say: A news report has a headline, a byline, and a first paragraph that answers who, what, where, when and why.
lesson.html:
• Headline: a short, catchy title
  • Byline: who wrote it
  • Lead paragraph: answers who, what, where, when and often why
  • Quotes: the exact words someone said, inside quotation marks
  • Written in the past tense, because it already happened

lesson.say: Read the report about the beach clean-up. It is a made-up report for this lesson.
lesson.html:
A made-up news report for this lesson

Learners collect 300 kg of litter from beach

By a Seaview Times reporter

Grade 5 learners from Seaview Primary School collected 300 kilograms of litter from the beach near their school last Saturday morning.

The 64 learners spent three hours picking up plastic bottles, bottle tops and fishing line. They wanted to protect the birds and fish that live along the coast.

"We found a seagull tangled in fishing line, and a lifeguard helped to free it," said learner Amahle Dube. "That is when we knew our work really mattered."

The school plans to clean the beach again next term.

steps: "When" asks about time.
Look in the lead paragraph.
It happened "last Saturday morning".

questions.q: Who collected the litter?
hints: "Who" is answered in the first paragraph.
They go to Seaview Primary School.
questions.explain: Grade 5 learners from Seaview Primary School collected the litter.

questions.q: Why did the learners clean the beach?
options: To protect the birds and fish
Because it was a school rule
hints: Find the sentence that starts "They wanted…"
It is about animals along the coast.
questions.explain: They wanted to protect the birds and fish along the coast.

questions.q: What is the job of the headline?
options: To tell the main news in a few words
To show the price of the paper
hints: It is the first thing you read.
questions.explain: A headline tells the main news quickly, so readers want to read on.

questions.q: Which sentence is a direct quote?
options: "We found a seagull tangled in fishing line," said Amahle.
The school plans to clean the beach again.
hints: A quote shows someone's exact words.
questions.explain: The quote has quotation marks and "said", showing Amahle's exact words.

questions.q: Sort the facts from the report.
hints: The amount and the school answer "what" and "who".
questions.explain: The amount and the school are what and who, last Saturday is when, and the beach is where.

reflect.q: What helped you find the facts?

units.parent: Your child read a news report and found who, what, where, when and why, and a direct quote.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of news text features, retrieval of the 5 Ws, purpose of headlines and recognition of direct speech.
units.done: News reports give the most important facts first.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Poetry: My Gogo
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 English Home Language, Term 1: Poetry (reading and viewing); figurative language: similes
units.intention: Today I am practising noticing and making similes.
units.prompt: What picture did that simile give you?
units.passage:
My Gogo (a 2to.iQ poem)

My gogo's hands are as soft as bread dough,
They move like a breeze when she plaits my hair slow.
Her laugh is like thunder that rolls round the room,
Her voice is as warm as the sun after gloom.

Her stories are as long as the road to the sea,
And her hugs are like blankets wrapped warmly round me.

lesson.say: Read the poem about a grandmother, called Gogo.
lesson.html:
My Gogo (a 2to.iQ poem)

My gogo's hands are as soft as bread dough,
They move like a breeze when she plaits my hair slow.
Her laugh is like thunder that rolls round the room,
Her voice is as warm as the sun after gloom.

Her stories are as long as the road to the sea,
And her hugs are like blankets wrapped warmly round me.

lesson.say: A simile compares two different things using like or as. Her hugs are like blankets.
lesson.html:
A simile compares two different things using like or as … as.

  • Her hugs are like blankets.
  • Her hands are as soft as bread dough.

Similes help the reader picture something and feel how the poet feels.

example.q: In "Her laugh is like thunder", what is being compared?
steps: Find the word "like".
On one side is "her laugh". On the other side is "thunder".
Her laugh is compared to thunder, because it is loud and fills the room.

questions.q: Which line contains a simile?
options: Her voice is as warm as the sun after gloom
hints: It compares her voice to something else.
questions.explain: "As warm as the sun" compares her voice to the sun.

questions.q: "Her hands are as soft as bread dough." What does this tell us?
options: Her hands are gentle and soft
Her hands are covered in flour
hints: What does bread dough feel like?
The poet compares how her hands feel.
Soft dough is gentle to touch.
questions.explain: Her hands feel soft and gentle, like bread dough.

questions.q: Why does the poet compare Gogo's hugs to blankets?
options: Her hugs feel warm and safe
hints: How does a blanket make you feel?
Hugs can make us feel the same.
questions.explain: Blankets are warm and comforting, and so are her hugs.

questions.q: Complete the simile: "The child ran as fast as ___."
hints: You need something that is very fast.
Which animal is famous for speed?
questions.explain: A cheetah is very fast, so it makes a good simile for speed.

questions.q: Sort these sentences: simile or not a simile?
items: He is as tall as a tree
hints: A simile compares two different things.
questions.explain: "As tall as a tree" and "like a bird" are similes. The others only describe.

reflect.q: What helped you understand the similes?

units.parent: Your child read a poem about a grandmother and learnt how similes help us picture things.
units.teacher: Shows recognition and interpretation of similes, inference about tone, and generating an apt comparison.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Life cycles
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 1, Life and Living: Life cycles (check against the Grade 5 ATP)
units.intention: Today I am practising putting the stages of a life cycle in order.
units.prompt: Why do you think it is called a cycle?

lesson.say: A life cycle shows the stages a living thing goes through, from the start of its life until it makes young of its own.
lesson.html: A life cycle shows the stages a living thing goes through, from the start of its life until it reproduces. Then the cycle starts again, which is why it is called a cycle.

lesson.say: A frog goes from egg to tadpole to froglet to adult frog. A butterfly goes from egg to caterpillar to pupa to adult butterfly.
lesson.html:
Frog:

egg→tadpole→froglet→adult frog

Butterfly:

egg→caterpillar (larva)→pupa→adult butterfly

Inside the pupa, the caterpillar's body changes completely. Big changes like this are called metamorphosis.

lesson.say: A plant grows from a seed into a seedling, then an adult plant, which makes flowers and new seeds.
lesson.html: seed→seedling→adult plant→flower→new seeds

example.q: Where does a tadpole fit in a frog's life cycle?
steps: A frog's life cycle starts with an egg in water.
A tadpole hatches from the egg and lives in water, breathing with gills.
So the tadpole comes after the egg and before the froglet.

questions.q: Put a frog's life cycle in order.
hints: Start with what the mother frog lays.
The tadpole lives in water and has a tail.
A froglet has legs and a short tail.
questions.explain: egg → tadpole → froglet → adult frog.

questions.q: Put a butterfly's life cycle in order.
hints: What hatches out and eats leaves?
The pupa comes just before the adult.
questions.explain: egg → caterpillar → pupa → adult butterfly.

questions.q: What happens inside a pupa?
options: The caterpillar's body changes into a butterfly
hints: The pupa comes between caterpillar and butterfly.
questions.explain: Inside the pupa, the caterpillar's body changes completely into a butterfly.

questions.q: Why is it called a life CYCLE?
options: The adult makes young, and the stages begin again
hints: What does an adult frog do?
The eggs start the stages again.
questions.explain: Adults make young, so the stages repeat in a circle: a cycle.

questions.q: Which comes straight after a seed in a plant's life cycle?
hints: What grows first when a seed germinates?
It is a very young plant.
questions.explain: A seed germinates and grows into a seedling.

reflect.q: What helped you remember the order?

units.parent: Your child put the stages of frog, butterfly and plant life cycles in order.
units.teacher: Shows sequencing of developmental stages, understanding of metamorphosis, and of why the pattern is cyclical.
units.done: Every living thing has a life cycle.

units.subject: Natural Sciences and Technology
units.title: Metals and non-metals
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Natural Sciences and Technology, Term 2, Matter and Materials: Metals and non-metals, uses of metals (check against the Grade 5 ATP)
units.intention: Today I am practising choosing the right material for a job.
units.prompt: Why is that material a good choice?

lesson.say: Metals are usually shiny, strong and hard. They let heat and electricity pass through them, and they can be bent or hammered into shape.
lesson.html:
Most metals (iron, copper, aluminium, gold) are:

  • shiny when polished
  • strong and hard
  • conductors: they let heat and electricity pass through
  • able to be bent and hammered into shapes

lesson.say: Non-metals such as wood, plastic, glass and rubber usually do not let heat or electricity through. That makes them good insulators.
lesson.html:
Non-metals such as wood, plastic, glass and rubber usually do not let heat or electricity through. They are insulators.

A pot is made of metal so heat reaches the food, but its handle is plastic or wood so you don't burn your hand.

example.q: Why are electric wires made of copper covered in plastic?
steps: Copper is a metal, so electricity passes through it easily.
Plastic is an insulator, so electricity does not pass through it.
The copper carries the electricity, and the plastic keeps people safe from shocks.

questions.q: Sort these materials into metals and non-metals.
hints: Metals are usually shiny and conduct heat.
Iron, copper and aluminium are used in pots, wires and cans.
Wood, plastic and glass do not conduct heat well.
questions.explain: Iron, copper and aluminium are metals. Wood, plastic and glass are non-metals.

questions.q: Why is a cooking pot made of metal?
options: Metal lets heat pass through to the food
hints: What does a pot need to do on the stove?
Metals are good conductors of heat.
questions.explain: Metals conduct heat, so heat passes through the pot to cook the food.

questions.q: Why does a pot have a wooden or plastic handle?
options: They are insulators, so the handle stays cool
hints: You don't want to burn your hand.
Which materials do not let heat through?
questions.explain: Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle does not get too hot.

questions.q: Which material would you use for the outside of an electric plug?
hints: You touch the outside of a plug.
It must not let electricity through to your hand.
questions.explain: Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps you safe from electric shocks.

questions.q: Which property lets metal be shaped into a car door?
options: It can be bent and hammered
hints: A car door is a curved shape.
How do you change the shape of metal?
Metals can be pressed and bent.
questions.explain: Metals can be bent and hammered into shapes like car doors.

reflect.q: How did you choose the right material?

units.parent: Your child learnt the properties of metals and non-metals and how we choose materials for a job.
units.teacher: Shows classification by properties, understanding of conductors and insulators, and reasoning about material choice for function and safety.
units.done: Engineers choose materials by what they need to do.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: Giving and receiving feedback
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: giving and receiving feedback
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Giving and receiving feedback (positive and negative, from peers and adults)
units.intention: Today I am practising giving kind, helpful feedback and receiving it well.
units.prompt: Would that feedback help someone improve?

lesson.say: Good feedback is kind, specific and helpful. Try two stars and a wish: two things that went well and one thing to improve.
lesson.html:
Good feedback is kind, specific and helpful. Try two stars and a wish:

  • ★ Something that went well
  • ★ Another thing that went well
  • ✦ A wish: one thing that could be better

"Your drawing is nice" is kind but not specific. "The colours in your sky really show it is sunset" is kind and specific.

lesson.say: When you get feedback, listen without interrupting, say thank you, and think about what you could use.
lesson.html:
• Listen without interrupting
  • Say thank you
  • Ask a question if something is not clear
  • Decide what you will use to improve

Feedback is about the work, not about who you are as a person.

example.q: Give Zola two stars and a wish about her poster.
steps: Star: "Your heading is big and easy to read."
Star: "Your pictures match the facts."
Wish: "I wish the writing at the bottom was a bit bigger."

questions.q: Which feedback is the most helpful?
options: "Your story's beginning hooked me. Maybe add more about how the boy felt."
hints: It says what went well and what to improve.
Which answer gives a clear idea for next time?
questions.explain: It names something specific that worked and gives a clear idea to improve.

questions.q: Sort these: specific feedback or vague feedback?
items: "Your handwriting is neat and easy to read"
hints: "Nice" and "Good job" don't say what was good.
questions.explain: Comments about the handwriting and labels are specific. "Nice" and "Good job" are vague.

questions.q: Your teacher says your maths needs more working out. What is a good way to respond?
options: "Thank you. I'll show my steps next time."
hints: Receiving feedback well means listening and thanking.
Which answer shows you will use it?
questions.explain: Thanking the teacher and planning to show your steps shows you can use feedback.

questions.q: What should feedback be about?
hints: It is not about who you are.
questions.explain: Feedback is about the work, so people can improve without feeling attacked.

questions.q: Which is a "wish" in two stars and a wish?
options: "I wish your title was a bit bigger."
hints: Which one helps them make it better?
questions.explain: "I wish your title was a bit bigger" suggests a helpful improvement.

units.parent: Your child practised giving kind, specific feedback and receiving feedback calmly.
units.teacher: Shows distinction between specific and vague feedback, constructive suggestions, and appropriate responses to feedback from adults.

units.subject: Life Skills
units.title: Safe and healthy relationships
units.topic: Personal and Social Well-being: relationships with peers, older people and strangers
units.caps: CAPS Grade 5 Life Skills, Term 1, Personal and Social Well-being: Relationships with peers, older people and strangers (safe and unsafe, good and bad relationships)
units.intention: Today I am practising telling safe relationships from unsafe ones.
units.prompt: How would that make you feel?

lesson.say: In a healthy relationship, people are kind, honest and respectful. They listen to each other and you feel safe.
lesson.html: In a healthy relationship with a friend or an adult, people are kind, honest and respectful. They listen, they keep you safe, and you feel good being with them.

lesson.say: Be careful if someone asks you to keep secrets, makes you feel scared, or asks for personal information. Never go anywhere with a stranger, and check with a trusted adult first.
lesson.html:
Warning signs: someone asks you to keep secrets from your family, makes you feel scared or uncomfortable, pressures you, or asks for personal information.

  • Never go anywhere with a stranger, even if they seem kind
  • Don't share your address, school or photos online
  • Always check with a trusted adult first
  • Tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong

example.q: Someone Bongi met online asks for her home address so they can send a gift. What should she do?
steps: Notice the warning sign: a person she doesn't know is asking for personal information.
Don't share the address, and don't reply further.
Tell a trusted adult and show them the message.

questions.q: Sort these: signs of a healthy relationship, or warning signs?
items: Asks you to keep secrets from your family
hints: Secrets from family are a warning sign.
Feeling scared is a warning sign.
questions.explain: Listening and respecting "no" are healthy. Secrets from family and feeling scared are warning signs.

questions.q: A stranger in a car says your mom sent him to fetch you. What should you do?
options: Don't go. Go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult
hints: Your family would tell you about any change of plan.
Go to a safe place, like back into school.
questions.explain: Never go with a stranger. Go to a safe place and tell a trusted adult.

questions.q: What information is safe to share with a new online friend?
options: A photo in your school uniform
hints: Personal information could tell someone where to find you.
Which answer does not reveal where you are?
questions.explain: A favourite book doesn't tell anyone where you are. Your address, school and uniform photos do.

questions.q: How do you show respect to older people?
hints: How do you greet a gogo or a neighbour?
questions.explain: Greeting older people and listening politely shows respect.

questions.q: Your friend always makes fun of you in front of others, then says it's "just a joke". What is true?
options: A good friend wouldn't keep hurting you. You can talk to a trusted adult
hints: Does it feel good or bad?
questions.explain: Repeated hurtful "jokes" are not healthy. You can say how it feels and talk to a trusted adult.

reflect.q: What would you do if something felt wrong?

units.parent: Your child learnt to recognise safe and unsafe relationships, online safety and stranger safety. Please talk about trusted adults at home.
units.teacher: Protective, scenario-based content. If a learner discloses anything, follow your school's safeguarding procedure.
units.done: Safe people respect you. You can always ask for help.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
units.caps: Cambridge Primary Mathematics (0096), Stage 5: Number (equivalence of simple fractions, decimals and percentages)
units.intention: Today I am matching fractions, decimals and percentages.
units.prompt: What does 50% off mean in a shop?

lesson.say: One half can be written as a fraction, a half, as a decimal, 0.5, or as a percentage, 50 percent. They all mean the same amount.
lesson.html: 1/2→0.5→50%

lesson.say: A quarter is 0.25, or 25 percent. Three quarters is 0.75, or 75 percent. One tenth is 0.1, or 10 percent.
lesson.html: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%→3/4 = 0.75 = 75%→1/10 = 0.1 = 10%

lesson.say: Per cent means out of 100. 30 percent means 30 out of 100, which is 0.3.

steps: Make the bottom 100: multiply top and bottom by 20.

questions.q: Which is the same as 1/2?
Write 0.25 as a fraction.
Write 70% as a decimal.
Write 3/10 as a percentage. (Type the number only.)

units.parent: Your child matched fractions, decimals and percentages.
units.teacher: Shows recognising equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages, including tenths, quarters and halves.

units.subject: English
units.title: Fact and opinion
units.caps: Cambridge Primary English (0058), Stage 5: Reading (distinguishing between fact and opinion)
units.intention: Today I am telling facts from opinions.
units.prompt: Is 'pizza is the best food' a fact?

lesson.say: A fact can be checked and proved true. For example: the Orange River is the longest river in South Africa.
lesson.html: Fact: can be proved.

lesson.say: An opinion is what someone thinks or feels. People can disagree. For example: the Orange River is the most beautiful river.
lesson.html: Opinion: what someone thinks.

lesson.say: Opinion words include best, worst, beautiful, I think and should.
lesson.html: best→worst→I think→should

example.q: Fact or opinion: 'Cheetahs can run faster than lions.'
steps: Can it be checked?
Yes, by measuring their speeds.
It is a fact.

questions.q: 'There are seven days in a week.' Is this a fact or an opinion?
questions.explain: It can be checked, so it is a fact.

questions.q: 'Saturday is the best day of the week.' Is this a fact or an opinion?
questions.explain: 'Best' shows an opinion.

questions.q: Which word often signals an opinion?
questions.explain: 'Beautiful' is a judgement.

questions.q: Sort the sentences.
hints: Boiling point and Durban can be checked.
questions.explain: The boiling point and Durban's location are facts; the others are opinions.

units.parent: Your child learnt to tell facts from opinions.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing fact from opinion and recognising evaluative language.
units.done: A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks.

units.subject: Science
units.title: Sound and vibrations
units.caps: Cambridge Primary Science (0097), Stage 5: Physics (sound is made by vibrations; pitch and loudness)
units.intention: Today I am finding out how sounds are made and changed.
units.prompt: Put your hand on your throat and hum. What do you feel?

lesson.say: Sound is made when something vibrates, moving quickly back and forth. When you hum, your vocal cords vibrate.
lesson.html: Sound comes from vibrations.

lesson.say: Bigger vibrations make louder sounds. Hitting a drum harder makes it louder.
lesson.html: Bigger vibrations → louder

lesson.say: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Faster vibrations make a higher pitch. A short, tight string gives a higher note than a long, loose one.
lesson.html: Fast vibration: high pitch→Slow vibration: low pitch

example.q: How can you make a guitar string play a higher note?
steps: A higher note needs faster vibrations.
Shorten the string by pressing it, or tighten it.
The string vibrates faster, so the pitch is higher.

questions.q: What makes a sound?
hints: Feel your throat when you hum.
questions.explain: Sounds come from vibrations.

questions.q: How do you make a drum louder?
questions.explain: Hitting harder makes bigger vibrations.

questions.q: Which string makes the higher note?
questions.explain: Short, tight strings vibrate faster: higher pitch.

questions.q: What is pitch?
options: How high or low a sound is
questions.explain: Pitch is how high or low a sound is.

units.parent: Your child learnt how sounds are made and how pitch and loudness change.
units.teacher: Shows explaining sound as vibration and relating vibration size and speed to loudness and pitch.
units.done: Bigger vibrations: louder. Faster vibrations: higher pitch.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Area and perimeter
units.caps: IB PYP Mathematics: measurement (perimeter and area of rectangles)
units.intention: Today I am finding the perimeter and area of rectangles.
units.prompt: How much fencing would a school garden need?

lesson.say: Central idea: Measuring space helps us plan and build. Key concept: Function. Today we are thinkers.
lesson.html:
Central idea: Measuring space helps us plan and build.

Key concept: Function · Learner profile: Thinkers

lesson.say: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. Add up all the sides. A rectangle 5 metres by 3 metres has a perimeter of 16 metres.
Area is the space inside a shape, measured in squares. Multiply length by width: 5 times 3 is 15 square metres.

example.q: A garden bed is 6 m long and 2 m wide. Find the perimeter and area.
steps: Perimeter: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 m.
Area: 6 × 2 = 12 m².
Fencing needs 16 m; soil covers 12 m².

questions.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 4 m by 2 m, in metres.
Find the area of a rectangle 7 cm by 3 cm, in cm².
You want to put a fence around a field. What do you need?
questions.explain: A fence goes around, so you need the perimeter.

questions.q: You want to cover a floor with tiles. What do you need?
questions.explain: Tiles cover the space inside: the area.

units.parent: Your child worked out the perimeter and area of rectangles.
units.teacher: Shows calculating perimeter and area of rectangles and choosing the right measure for a task (thinker).

units.subject: Language
units.title: Writing a news report
units.caps: IB PYP Language: writing (news reports: headline, the five Ws, and order of importance)
units.intention: Today I am writing a news report.
units.prompt: What news happened at school this week?

lesson.say: Central idea: News reports tell people what happened, clearly and fairly. Key concept: Responsibility. Today we are principled.
lesson.html:
Central idea: News reports tell people what happened, clearly and fairly.

Key concept: Responsibility · Learner profile: Principled

lesson.say: A news report answers who, what, where, when and why in the first paragraph.
lesson.html: Who?→What?→Where?→When?→Why?

lesson.say: A headline is short and grabs attention. The most important facts come first, then the details. A good reporter checks facts and stays fair.
lesson.html: Learners Clean Up Riverbank

example.q: Write a first sentence for a report about a school clean-up.
steps: Who: Grade 5 learners. What: cleaned the river. Where: Mngeni River.
When: on Friday. Why: to protect wildlife.
'On Friday, Grade 5 learners cleaned the banks of the Mngeni River to protect wildlife.'

questions.q: What is a headline?
options: A short title that grabs attention
questions.explain: A headline is a short, attention-grabbing title.

questions.q: Which question is NOT one of the five Ws?
questions.explain: The five Ws are who, what, where, when and why.

questions.q: What comes first in a news report?
questions.explain: The most important facts come first.

questions.q: Why should a reporter check their facts?
options: So the report is true and fair
questions.explain: Reporters are responsible for telling the truth.

units.parent: Your child wrote a news report answering who, what, where, when and why.
units.teacher: Shows structuring a news report with headline and five Ws, and recognising the responsibility to report accurately (principled).
units.done: Headline, the five Ws first, then details. Check your facts.

units.subject: Social Studies
units.title: How communities share and trade
units.caps: IB PYP Social studies, transdisciplinary theme 'How we organise ourselves': how communities organise trade, money and services
units.intention: Today I am finding out how communities trade and share.
units.prompt: Where does the bread in your shop come from?

lesson.say: Our theme is How we organise ourselves. Central idea: Communities organise trade and services so people can meet their needs. Key concept: Connection. Today we are thinkers.
lesson.html:
Central idea: Communities organise trade and services so people can meet their needs.

Key concept: Connection · Learner profile: Thinkers

lesson.say: Needs are things we must have, like food, water and shelter. Wants are things we would like, like toys.
lesson.html: Needs: food, water, shelter→Wants: toys, games

lesson.say: Long ago, people swapped goods, called bartering. Today we usually use money, which makes trade easier. Shops, farms and transport are connected.
lesson.html: Farm grows wheat→Bakery makes bread→Truck delivers→Shop sells

example.q: Why is money easier than swapping?
steps: Swapping only works if both people want what the other has.
Money can be used to buy anything.
So money makes trade easier.

questions.q: Which is a need?
questions.explain: Water is a need.

questions.q: What is bartering?
questions.explain: Bartering is swapping goods directly.

questions.q: Put bread's journey in order.
questions.explain: Farm, bakery, truck, shop.

questions.q: What would happen if the trucks stopped running?
options: Shops would run out of bread
hints: The bread can't reach the shop.
questions.explain: Without delivery, shops can't get bread.

units.parent: Your child explored how communities trade and how goods reach shops.
units.teacher: How we organise ourselves: shows distinguishing needs and wants and explaining connections in a supply chain (thinker).
units.done: Communities are connected: farms, bakeries, transport and shops.
